preference_rationale:
Although focusing on the specific company is the most direct measure, I picked B because of my prior around how shortage cycles work. Prices move during shortages in some general way, and there must be indicators of whether a given episode is durable or a cycle peak that would be a mistake to invest in. B is built to find those indicators; A is built to price one company's paperwork.

On the heterogeneity worry: semis likely do not behave very differently across cycles once you account for the cause and the prevailing market regime, so pooling episodes within an industry is reasonable and the usual objection that twenty to thirty cross-industry cases are too few or too dissimilar does not apply here. B is ranking features by conditional base rate, not estimating a coefficient.

Weak because A is the more direct measurement and someone still has to do that work before a position goes on.
critique_A:
It tiers agreements on contract attributes - minimum quantities, take-or-pay damages, cancellability, RPO inclusion - when these indicators need to be industry and market-regime specific. Contract language is not what separates the agreements that hold from the ones that reprice; switching cost and requalification lag are, which is why aerospace forgings and container slots behave differently at identical contract strength. A sorts on the wrong axis.

The explicit numeric thresholds seem arbitrary. The 90-95 / 70 / 25-35 percent tier haircuts, and the six constructive conditions (60% NTM coverage, 40% year-two, cash support 15%, top-three customer share under 45%, mirror reconciliation 50%, modeled horizon two years beyond market-implied), are all asserted rather than derived.

The haircuts are calibrated off a single prior episode, 2021-23 semiconductors. That is the one-observation base rate this plan is implicitly arguing is sufficient, and it is an episode where agreements broke on price - potentially the wrong prior to carry into a different industry.
critique_B:
The knock is all the datasets listed in the plan - TrendForce, Fastmarkets, UxC, Argus/ICIS, Drewry/Xeneta, Panjiva, PACER, the SEMI fab database. This firm would need to cobble together the data points individually using its analysts rather than subscribe to all those vendors to answer this one question. The plan should be built around that constraint instead of assuming the subscriptions.

The objection that twenty to thirty episodes across ten industries is too few or too heterogeneous does not apply, and a review raising it would be misapplying a standard concern. B ranks features by conditional base rate rather than regressing, and behavior within an industry is reasonably stable across cycles once cause and regime are accounted for.
why_loser_was_defensible: Focusing on the specific company is the most direct measure of the question actually asked, and A is the only plan that produces a priced answer for the name in front of you rather than a framework to apply to it.
